project.title: Release eval - Brackenridge graded foam filters

sections.s242:
The technical uncertainty was whether a sponge-replicated alumina foam with a pore gradient through a 50 mm part could survive firing and perform in a pour, and the team calls this graded structure the cascade-fired lattice. Dunmore Falls Ceramics is a foam-ceramic filter manufacturer for metal foundries. The company set out to make a filter that resists cracking in the pour and captures more fine inclusions, though whether breakage or capture was the main driver was disputed. It has made these filters for a little over twenty years at its Dunmore Falls, Ontario plant, with about 60 people. That sponge-replication experience gave it direct knowledge of how slurry loading and firing govern filter structure.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to build a pore gradient into a replicated foam was insufficient. Published graded foams are mostly lab scale, small discs made by gel casting or freeze casting, not sponge replication. No shrinkage data existed for parts where slurry loading, pore size and viscosity change across 50 mm. Interface stress depends on strut geometry on both sides, which could not be modelled well because the struts are hollow after the sponge burns out.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of whether a graded replicated foam survives firing given different slurry pick-up and shrinkage, for the purposes of creating a graded filter with better fine-inclusion capture and thermal shock resistance at near-standard flow.

It was uncertain whether a 10 ppi and 30 ppi template would survive firing without separating, because different pore sizes pick up different slurry amounts and the shrinkage mismatch at the interface was unknown. It was also uncertain whether a gradient could raise capture of 20 to 80 micron inclusions without cutting flow more than 10 percent, because finer pores raise flow resistance and priming head. Finally, it remained uncertain whether the graded interface would arrest or initiate cracks under thermal shock, since published results on graded interfaces differ by material.
sections.s244:
The technical uncertainty was whether a sponge-replicated alumina foam with a two-zone pore gradient could survive firing, because different pore sizes pick up different slurry amounts and the shrinkage mismatch at the interface was unknown. To test whether a graded foam survives firing, the team planned a 10 ppi and 30 ppi two-zone template, 50 mm thick, and a staged program. Phase one would make graded green bodies that survive firing. Phase two would test flow and capture on the survivors. Phase three would cover thermal shock and burst testing, then a pour trial. The program started August 18 2025, and the technician was full time from September 2 2025.

It was hypothesized that if both zones carry similar slurry mass per volume, achieved by adjusting slurry viscosity in a 10 ppi entry and 30 ppi exit template, then linear firing shrinkage across the interface will match within 0.5 percent and the part will survive firing without delamination. If the part survives, it should capture at least 30 percent more 20 to 80 micron inclusions than the standard 20 ppi filter at a flow rate no more than 10 percent lower. A trial with shrinkage mismatch above 0.5 percent, or with frequent delamination, would disprove the first clause.

The team could not tell if bonded templates would survive firing, so trial 1 (September 2025) used adhesive bonding. It bonded 25 mm sheets of 10 ppi and 30 ppi sponge with polyurethane adhesive. It then coated 24 parts of 75x75x50 mm in a single dip of standard alumina slurry at about 2,400 mPa.s. The parts were fired at a 1,580 C peak with a 2 h hold. Eighteen of 24 delaminated at the bond line, with 1.4 percent shrinkage mismatch on the survivors. The finer sponge picked up much more slurry per volume, and the adhesive left a burnout gap. The team therefore moved to thermal fusing of the sponges and a two-stage dip. The whole part went into thinner slurry at about 1,500 mPa.s, then only the coarse half into 2,400 mPa.s slurry. Trial 2 (October to November 2025, 40 parts, standard firing) delaminated 9 parts, about 22 percent, with 0.7 percent shrinkage mismatch. Single-dip adhesive bonding was not viable, and the two-stage dip improved the mismatch but not enough for production.

The remaining mismatch exceeded the 0.5 percent target, so trial 3 (December 2025 to January 2026) kept the two-stage dip on 36 parts. It added a 1 C/min ramp between 1,100 and 1,350 C, the main sintering shrinkage range, and a 45 min hold at 1,350 C. Two of 36 parts delaminated, about 6 percent, and the shrinkage mismatch fell to 0.4 percent, within the 0.5 percent target. The slow ramp cost about 3 hours more kiln time per load. Mismatch was driven more by slurry mass per volume than by pore size. The slow ramp absorbed the remaining difference, and adhesive cannot work because it burns out before the ceramic sinters.

Later trials tested the graded filter in a flow rig and in thermal shock. In the February 2026 rig, with 50 kg of A356 per run at 720 C, the graded filter flowed at 3.8 kg/s against 4.1 kg/s for 20 ppi. It captured 41 percent more inclusions, though 2 of 6 pours choked late. Cutting the fine exit layer from 25 mm to 15 mm held 3.9 kg/s with 36 percent more capture. In thermal shock, graded parts retained 68 percent strength against 55 percent for 20 ppi, and a well-matched interface arrested a crack.
sections.s246:
The technical uncertainty was whether a graded filter could survive firing, and the objective was to understand how slurry pick-up and shrinkage govern that survival. The hypothesis was partly proven. The team could not tell if a graded foam would survive firing, and trial 3 met the 0.5 percent target with a shrinkage mismatch of 0.4 percent. It was not proven that matching slurry mass per volume alone is enough; a slower ramp through the sintering window was also needed.

The team determined that adhesive bonding with a single dip is not viable. The adhesive burns out before the ceramic sinters. Of 24 parts made in trial 1, 18 delaminated, with 1.4 percent shrinkage mismatch on the survivors. The team also established that shrinkage mismatch is driven more by slurry mass per volume than by pore size. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether a 10 ppi and 30 ppi template would survive firing without separating. Based on this understanding, the team used thermal fusing, a two-stage dip and a 1 C/min ramp from 1,100 to 1,350 C. In trial 3, that combination brought shrinkage mismatch to 0.4 percent, within the 0.5 percent target, and 2 of 36 parts delaminated.

A customer pour trial of 200 filters at one foundry showed no breakage. It is promising but covers one foundry and one alloy, so it does not yet confirm the result. Three questions stay open for fiscal 2027: whether the gradient works at 30 mm thickness, whether a continuous gradient can replace two zones, and whether a different slurry binder can shorten the slow ramp, which adds about 3 hours of kiln time per load. Each remains open because the work so far covers only the 50 mm two-zone part.

The team learned how to make a two-zone replicated foam survive firing without delamination, which answers the original goal of a graded filter for aluminium foundries. The two-stage dip, fused templates and slow ramp are the process changes that made this possible.

project.title: Release eval - Marrowgate cold-water biofilter control

sections.s242:
The company designs recirculating aquaculture systems for land-based trout farms. It was uncertain how to shorten nitrification start-up at water temperatures below 10 C, and the company set out to shorten it so clients can stock fish sooner. Its hands-on work building and commissioning these systems for cold-water rainbow trout and Arctic char, often at 6 to 12 C, gave it direct experience of how biofilters behave in cold water.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to shorten nitrification start-up at water temperatures below 10 C was insufficient. Standard practice was ammonium chloride dosing and waiting, or seeding with media from an existing biofilter, and neither showed how to speed bacterial community establishment in cold water. Below 10 C, nitrification start-up took 9 to 10 weeks, against 3 to 4 weeks at 20 C. Published work and the company's experience indicated that seed media from a warm system goes into shock in about 8 C water, where the bacteria survive but barely grow. No documented method existed for preparing seed media to establish nitrification quickly at these temperatures.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of how to shorten nitrification start-up at water temperatures below 10 C, for the purposes of creating a biofilter start-up method for cold-water recirculating aquaculture systems. The target was full nitrification in under 5 weeks at 8 C.

It was uncertain how to shorten nitrification start-up below 10 C, because bacteria are slow in cold water. It was uncertain whether seeding could help at all, because seed media from a warm system goes into shock in 8 C water. It was also uncertain whether stepwise acclimation of the seed media, at 1 C every 4 days from 14 to 8 C, would bring seeded biofilters to full nitrification in under 5 weeks. Whether a 10 percent seed fraction was adequate, and whether it would hold at 6 C, remained open, because cold-water growth rates left no basis for predicting the seed quantity required.
sections.s244:
The technological problem was how to shorten nitrification start-up below 10 C, where standard practice took 9 to 10 weeks and seed media from a warm system went into shock in cold water. The company planned a three-loop trial at 8 C to test whether acclimated seed shortens start-up. The trial ran in the pilot recirculating aquaculture system from September 8 to November 13, 2025, using independent loops, each with a 6 m3 fish tank and a 1.2 m3 moving bed biofilter. Loop A was unseeded and dosed with ammonium chloride. Loop B received 10 percent unacclimated seed from a 16 C system. Loop C received 10 percent seed that had undergone stepwise acclimation in a side tank from 14 C to 8 C at 1 C every 4 days. Full nitrification was defined as processing 1 mg/L of total ammonia nitrogen to under 0.2 mg/L in 24 hours with nitrite under 0.3 mg/L. Technicians ran daily water chemistry and pulled lab samples to confirm each reading.

It was hypothesized that if seed media is acclimated stepwise from 14 C to 8 C at 1 C every 4 days, then the seeded biofilter will reach full nitrification at 8 C in under 5 weeks, compared with the unseeded and unacclimated-seed loops run under the same conditions.

The first question was whether seeding could help at all, since seed media from a warm system goes into shock in 8 C water. The team put 10 percent mature media taken directly from a 16 C system into loop B and compared it with the unseeded loop A. Loop B reached full nitrification in 47 days against 66 days for loop A, so seeding helped. However, loop B stalled at the nitrite stage for 19 days, which showed that moving warm seed straight into cold water wasted much of its benefit. The team therefore changed the seed preparation, rather than the seed quantity, in loop C. The conclusion was that unacclimated seed suffers cold shock that stalls the nitrite stage, so direct transfer does not give a fast start-up.

The second question was whether stepwise acclimation would remove that stall. Loop C used the same 10 percent seed fraction, acclimated in the side tank before it went into the biofilter. It reached full nitrification in 31 days at 8 C, which met the target of under 5 weeks. Loop A took 66 days and loop B took 47 days, so acclimation roughly halved start-up compared with unacclimated seed. The nitrite stall in loop C was about 6 days, against 19 days in loop B. The conclusion was that stepwise acclimation of seed media shortens nitrification start-up at 8 C and avoids most of the stall seen with unacclimated seed.
sections.s246:
Shortening nitrification start-up below 10 C was uncertain, because seed media from a warm system goes into shock in 8 C water and standard practice took 9 to 10 weeks. The objective was to reach full nitrification in under 5 weeks at 8 C, and the experimental work achieved it. It was established that stepwise acclimation of seed media roughly halved start-up: loop C reached full nitrification in 31 days at 8 C, against 47 days for unacclimated seed and 66 days unseeded. The hypothesis was proven. Seeding helped even without acclimation, but acclimation made the difference between meeting the 5-week target and missing it.

sections.s242:
Grain Dryer Controls builds controllers and analytics software for grain dryers. The company set out to build an early-warning system that flags burner and column faults on grain dryers at least 15 minutes ahead.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge needed to warn of slow-developing faults in time was insufficient. Fixed threshold alarms are late, because plenum temperature crosses the threshold only when the fault is well along. No documented methods existed for separating slow drift from slow real faults without a trusted reference sensor or periodic calibration, which the company's dryers lack. Anomaly models trained on clean data flag drift as anomalies, and retraining on drifted data teaches the model that drift is normal, which can hide real slow faults. Plenum temperature sensors drift 1 to 3 degrees C per month and moisture sensors up to 1.5 points per month.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of how slow sensor drift can be separated from slow real faults, without labelled drift examples, in coupled industrial process data, for the purposes of giving operators early burner and column fault warnings on grain dryers with few false alarms.

It was uncertain whether sensor bias could be separated from real process change in a coupled dryer system, because burner output, air flow, grain flow, ambient conditions and grain moisture interact, and it was unknown whether the available sensors carried enough independent information to isolate bias.

It was also uncertain whether false alarms could stay low without losing detection lead time. Anything that makes the model more tolerant of slow change also makes it slower to see slow faults, and a gradually plugging column develops as slowly as drift does.
sections.s244:
The technical uncertainty was whether slow sensor drift could be separated from slow real faults in a coupled dryer process, with no labelled drift, no trusted reference sensor and no periodic calibration. False alarms also had to stay low and lead time long. The company planned four phases for fiscal 2026. These were a rebuilt baseline measured under drift, training with synthetic drift, an energy balance residual model with online bias tracking, and shadow mode trials on customer dryers during the fall 2025 harvest. To test whether false alarms could stay low without losing lead time, the team fixed definitions in July 2025 before any run. A false alarm was an alert with no fault in the following two hours, counted per dryer-day. Lead time ran from the alert to the earlier of the existing hard-limit alarm or manual operator shutdown.

It was hypothesized that if anomaly scores use energy balance residuals (expected plenum temperature from fuel rate, air flow and ambient temperature) with online bias tracking from sensor redundancy, then false alarms will stay below 0.25 per dryer per day with drift up to 3 degrees C per month. Median lead time on burner and column faults would also stay at least 15 minutes. A false alarm rate of 0.25 or more, or a median lead time under 15 minutes, would disprove it.

The first experiment asked how the fiscal 2025 isolation forest fails under drift. In July and August 2025 the team rebuilt it on 2024 data from 14 dryers (about 11,000 dryer-hours) and tested held-out data with injected drift of 1, 2 and 3 degrees C per month. False alarms per dryer-day were 0.3 at zero drift, 1.4 at 2 degrees per month by week four, and 2.6 at 3 degrees. The baseline caught 9 of 11 real faults with a median lead time of 9 minutes, so lead time was already short. The work also covered this: Billing portal migration to a new cloud host is routine IT work.

The second experiment tested whether the model could learn to ignore drift. In August 2025 the team injected random slow synthetic drift into the training data, 0.5 to 3 degrees C per month on temperatures and up to 1.5 points per month on moisture. False alarms fell to 0.6 per dryer-day, but the model caught only 6 of 11 faults. It missed all 3 column plugs, which develop over 30 to 60 minutes, because it treated slow rises as drift. The team dropped the approach, having confirmed that tolerance to slow change hides slow faults.

The third experiment aimed to separate drift from real process change. In September 2025 the team fit a per-dryer energy balance on the first 48 hours of the season, predicting plenum and exhaust temperature from fuel flow, fan speed, ambient temperature and humidity. A Kalman filter tracked slow bias per sensor, limited to 4 degrees C per month, using two plenum sensors and the ambient sensor. It updated only when the process was steady. On 2024 data with injected drift of 3 degrees per month, false alarms were 0.18 per dryer-day, 10 of 11 faults were caught including all three column plugs, and median lead time was 22 minutes. The miss was an igniter fault on a dryer with one plenum sensor, where the tracker absorbed the fault.

The fourth experiment tested field conditions. From October 6 to November 21, 2025, shadow mode ran on nine customer dryers, seven with two plenum sensors and two with one. The seven dual-sensor dryers averaged 0.21 false alarms per dryer-day, with measured drift up to 2.7 degrees C per month on one dryer. The two single-sensor dryers averaged 0.64. All four real events were flagged, with lead times of 14, 19, 26 and 31 minutes, so the 14-minute flame event fell under the 15-minute target. From January to March 2026 the team replayed fall data using exhaust temperature as an indirect second reference. Single-sensor false alarms fell from 0.64 to 0.33 per day, still above target.
sections.s246:
It was uncertain whether slow sensor drift could be separated from slow real faults without labelled drift or a trusted reference sensor. The investigation showed that energy balance residual scoring with online bias tracking works under realistic drift, while training on synthetic drift hides slow faults. The objective was largely achieved and the hypothesis partly proven. On the seven dual-sensor dryers, false alarms averaged 0.21 per dryer-day, below the 0.25 limit. Three of four field events met the 15-minute lead time target; the 14-minute flame event fell short. Moisture drift is not yet tracked with the same method.

An isolation forest on raw sensors fails under drift, reaching 2.6 false alarms per dryer-day at 3 degrees C per month. The baseline caught 9 of 11 faults with a median lead time of 9 minutes, so lead time was already short. Anything that makes a model more tolerant of slow change also makes it slower to see slow faults. Training on synthetic drift cut false alarms to 0.6 but caught only 6 of 11 faults, so the team dropped it.

Residual scoring with online bias tracking kept false alarms below 0.25 per dryer-day under drift. On 2024 data with injected drift of 3 degrees C per month, not live faults, false alarms were 0.18 per dryer-day, 10 of 11 faults were caught and median lead time was 22 minutes. Sensor redundancy decided the result: in the field trial, the two single-sensor dryers had 0.64 false alarms per dryer-day. A replay using exhaust temperature as an indirect second reference gave 0.33.

Single-sensor dryers remain above the 0.25 target at 0.33, because exhaust temperature only partly replaces a second plenum sensor. A second field trial at the Ashgrove elevator is booked for spring 2027. A full season with live alerts, flame event lead time and moisture drift also remain open.

sections.s242:
It was uncertain whether a window coating could be UV-clear, safe for drinking water and durable in chlorinated water, because most fluoropolymers and hydrogels lose 30 to 60 percent of transmission at 254 nm. The company designs and builds water-quality instruments for municipal treatment plants. It set out to build an in-line analyzer that stays accurate for at least 30 days between cleanings without a mechanical wiper. Orion-1, a wiper-equipped prototype, was built in fiscal 2025, and the team met the limits of existing knowledge directly.

Most fluoropolymers and hydrogels that resist fouling lose 30 to 60 percent of their transmission at 254 nm. Many anti-fouling coatings used on marine sensors are biocidal, which is unusable in drinking or wastewater, or absorb strongly in the UV. No published coating was found that combined UV clarity, drinking-water safety and chlorine durability. Existing understanding also treated fouling as attenuating light evenly across wavelengths, but biofilm contains organics that absorb in the UV, so a simple ratio correction had no established basis.

The objective was to advance understanding of UV-transparent anti-fouling window surfaces and dual-wavelength fouling compensation, to create an in-line 254 nm analyzer with fouling drift under 5 percent raw and within 2 percent corrected for at least 30 days without cleaning. The team sought to learn whether a window surface could resist biofilm attachment for 30 days or more while staying UV-clear at 254 nm.

It was also uncertain whether a coating could reach at least 85 percent transmission at 254 nm when new and survive chlorinated, gritty water, and whether a thin sol-gel layer with a fluorinated top surface could keep raw drift under 5 percent for 30 days. Finally, it was uncertain whether the 365 nm reference channel could track fouling at 254 nm as the biofilm aged, because the film's own UV-absorbing organics could change that relationship.
sections.s244:
The team did not know whether a window coating could be UV-clear at 254 nm, safe for drinking water and durable in chlorinated water. It could not find a published coating that combined all three. It therefore planned staged testing of candidate coatings to learn whether that combination existed. Coupon screening ran from August to October 2025 against uncoated controls. Bench testing of dual-wavelength correction in a fouling tank followed from October 2025 to January 2026. Field trials of full Orion-2 units at the Port Aldous Harbourside plant ran from February to June 2026. Each stage tested the previous stage's result under more realistic conditions.

If a thin silica sol-gel layer with a fluorinated top surface cuts biofilm attachment, then raw fouling drift will stay under 5 percent for 30 days, with initial transmission of at least 85 percent at 254 nm. A raw drift of 5 percent or more before day 30, or an initial transmission below 85 percent, would disprove it.

The team did not know if a coating could be UV-clear, safe and durable, so it screened four candidates. It coated fused silica coupons with a fluorosilane monolayer, a sol-gel with a fluorinated top, a zwitterionic polymer brush and a thin titania film. Twelve coupons of each, plus 12 uncoated controls, sat in a secondary effluent side stream for 42 days. Transmission at 254 nm was measured every 3 days. Uncoated windows lost 5 percent by day 11. The fluorosilane started at 92 percent transmission but wore off, reaching 5 percent loss by day 17. The zwitterionic brush resisted biofilm best but started at only 71 percent transmission. Titania grew film faster than the control; the team suspects the in-stream UV was too low to activate it and that its rough surface aided attachment. Only the sol-gel with fluorinated top met both targets, narrowly, starting at 89 percent transmission and reaching 5 percent loss at day 31.

Fouling started at the edges where the sol-gel was thinnest, so the team changed the dip withdrawal speed. It reduced withdrawal from 2 mm/s to 1 mm/s to give a more even layer of about 180 nm. A second round of 12 coupons was coated in November 2025. Time to 5 percent loss rose to 38 days. Initial transmission fell slightly to 87 percent, still above the 85 percent target. Why the slower withdrawal helped was not explained beyond this observation. The more even thickness delayed fouling while keeping clarity above target.

The fouling tank work tested whether a fixed multiple of 365 nm loss could correct 254 nm fouling drift. Six Orion-2 heads with uncoated windows ran 21 days in recirculated secondary effluent spiked with nutrients, which sped biofilm growth about threefold. Both channels were logged every 5 minutes. A window was pulled every 3 days to measure the film directly. The multiple was about 1.6 in the first 4 to 5 days and fell to about 1.15 after day 8. A fixed multiple of 1.4 therefore left 4.8 percent drift at day 21. The team then fitted a correction factor as a function of accumulated 365 nm loss, fitting on 4 heads and testing on the other 2. Held-out heads showed 1.7 percent drift at day 21. A fresh test of 6 new heads in January 2026 gave 1.9 percent worst case. The fixed-ratio hypothesis was disproved, but a correction keyed to accumulated reference loss held drift under 2 percent over 21 days in the tank.

Four complete Orion-2 units with coated windows and the fitted correction factor ran at Harbourside from February 9 to June 12, 2026. Two ran on secondary effluent and two on chlorinated final effluent. Twice-weekly grab samples on a lab spectrophotometer served as reference. On secondary effluent, raw drift crossed 5 percent at day 36 and day 40, while corrected drift stayed under 2 percent until day 52 and day 55. On final effluent, one unit's coating began thinning after about 70 days, with a 9 percent non-biofilm transmission drop between day 70 and day 90. Chlorine is suspected of slowly attacking the fluorinated layer, but this was not confirmed.
sections.s246:
It was uncertain whether a UV-clear anti-fouling window and a reference channel could hold fouling drift under 5 percent raw and within 2 percent corrected for 30 days. The objective was partly achieved. The team did not know if a coating could be UV-clear and durable, and a sol-gel with a fluorinated top met both targets. Withdrawn at 1 mm/s instead of 2 mm/s, it gave a layer of about 180 nm, 87 percent initial transmission and 38 days to 5 percent loss. The fixed-multiple hypothesis was disproved.

It was determined that only one of four screened coatings met both targets. The team did not know if a coating could be UV-clear, safe and durable. The sol-gel with fluorinated top started at 89 percent transmission and lost 5 percent at day 31. The zwitterionic brush resisted biofilm best but started at 71 percent transmission, so it failed the clarity target. The sol-gel was carried into Orion-2.

It was established that the 254/365 multiple is not constant: it fell from about 1.6 to about 1.15 as the film matured. A fixed 1.4 multiple left 4.8 percent drift at day 21. A correction factor fitted to accumulated 365 nm loss gave 1.7 percent drift on held-out heads and 1.9 percent worst case on six new heads. In the field on secondary effluent, corrected drift stayed under 2 percent until day 52 and day 55. Raw drift crossed 5 percent at day 36 and day 40.

Coating durability in chlorinated water beyond 70 days is unresolved. One final-effluent unit lost 9 percent transmission between day 70 and day 90. Chlorine attack on the fluorinated layer is suspected but not confirmed, so fiscal 2027 work must test whether it is the cause. Cold-water behaviour at 4 to 6 C and transfer of the correction factor to a second plant also remain unknown.

With the sol-gel and the correction factor, Orion-2 moved toward an in-line analyzer that holds calibration past 30 days without a wiper on secondary effluent.

sections.s242:
Kessridge, Ontario is home to a company that finishes MDF panels for other companies. The company set out to offer customers a solvent-free powder finish on thick routed MDF doors. Its process engineer had automotive powder-line experience on steel, but the company had run no powder panels before July 2025.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to powder coat thick routed MDF was insufficient. Datasheet low-temperature powders were shown only for thin flat panels, not 25 mm routed MDF. No published data existed for the panel surface temperature at which outgassing defects start on this board, and preheating to bring moisture to the surface is itself heat.

The aim of this work was to learn how to make 25 mm routed MDF conductive without triggering outgassing defects, for the purpose of a powder finishing process running at 2.5 metres per minute with full cure at a panel surface temperature of 120 C or less.

It was not known at the outset whether the board could be made conductive without a preheat that triggers outgassing defects. The moisture that gives conductivity is the same moisture that outgasses, so one setting for both was doubtful. Outgassing defects started at about 118 to 122 C whatever the dwell time, leaving little room for a powder cure. It also remained uncertain whether any low-temperature powder could cure fully below that point with a cure window of at least 8 C.
sections.s244:
The team's workplan separated the two heat-dependent problems, conductivity and cure, and tested each against the 120 C panel surface temperature ceiling. Thermocouples logged panel surface temperature on every test panel, and the team changed one thing at a time so each result could be attributed to a single variable. Film build, outgassing defects, MEK double rubs and cross-hatch adhesion were measured on each set of panels.

It was hypothesized that if a conductive edge sealer is applied to the routed edges, then preheat can fall below 110 C and edge coverage can reach at least 60 microns, with at most 1 outgassing defect per square metre. A preheat that stays at 110 C or an edge coverage under 60 microns would disprove it.

Trial 1 followed the supplier datasheet on 25 mm routed MDF: IR preheat to 110 C, a standard low-temperature powder and 10 minutes at 135 C oven air. Panel surface temperature reached 131 C, outgassing defects averaged 14 per square metre overall and 30 on the routed edges, and edge film build was 35 microns against 82 on the faces. The datasheet figure had been shown only for flat panels, so the process did not transfer.

Trial 2 kept the preheat, lowered oven air to 125 C and extended dwell from 10 to 14 minutes. Peak panel surface temperature was 121 C and outgassing defects fell to 4 per square metre, but cure was incomplete at 30 MEK double rubs. Raising the air 2 C brought outgassing defects back to 9 per square metre, and the onset did not move with dwell time. The powder did not cure below about 122 C while edge outgassing began above about 120 C, so outgassing defects followed peak panel surface temperature, not dwell time.

Trial 3 applied a water-based conductive edge sealer to the routed edges only, flash-dried 6 minutes at 60 C, and cut preheat from 110 C to 85 C. Edge film build averaged 58 microns (minimum 47) and outgassing defects fell to 1.8 per square metre. Overspray onto the faces reduced cross-hatch adhesion to 3B against a 5B target on 12 percent of panels; an edge-only nozzle and a face mask restored 5B.

In Trial 4, with the supplier, the team ran a fast-catalysed powder at three catalyst levels with the sealer in place. The fastest level cut gel time from 210 s to 95 s at 125 C and cured fully at 120 C in 9 minutes, but its orange peel was 5 against a target of 6. Splitting the oven dwell into ramp and hold zones cut overshoot from about 5 C to 2 C, giving a cure window of 113 to 121 C. Across 140 panels, edge film build averaged 64 microns (minimum 52) and outgassing defects averaged 0.6 per square metre.

Trial 5 ran 600 doors at 2.5 metres per minute. Outgassing defects averaged 0.9 per square metre, but 13 percent of deep cove doors had edge coverage below 60 microns, while no shaker panels did.
sections.s246:
The aim was to learn how to make 25 mm routed MDF conductive without triggering outgassing defects, with full cure at a panel surface temperature of 120 C or less. This was partly achieved. An edge sealer can give the conductivity that preheat used to give, so preheat came down by 25 C (110 C to 85 C). The deep cove profile did not reach the target.

Preheat heat itself caused the outgassing defects. The supplier process, with a preheat to 110 C, gave a panel surface temperature of 131 C and 30 outgassing defects per square metre on the routed edges. Lowering oven air and lengthening dwell showed that outgassing defects followed peak panel surface temperature, not dwell time, starting at about 118 to 122 C. This resolved the uncertainty about whether the board could be made conductive without a preheat that triggers outgassing defects. The company then applied a conductive edge sealer, which gave an average edge coverage of 58 microns and 1.8 outgassing defects per square metre.

Shaker doors are ready for production, but the deep cove profile is not. In the pilot, 13 percent of deep cove doors had edge coverage below 60 microns. It remains uncertain whether a different sealer, gun angle or cove geometry can fix this, because the concave shape shields itself from the charge. Further deep cove trials are planned for fiscal 2027.
